title: Meaningful work is a strong Gen Z aspiration constrained by pay, financial security and care-work conditions
source_unit: Harvard Graduate School of Education Making Caring Common, in collaboration with Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation, as reported by Harvard Gazette, Gen Z puts high priority on jobs with meaning, purpose, but sees daunting hurdles, August 3, 2026
geography: United States; Gen Z respondents born 1997–2012, including adults ages 18–29 in work and wellbeing analyses

observations.period: 2026; Gen Z work aspirations and current job alignment

denominator.unit: representative sample of people born 1997–2012 in the Making Caring Common/Gallup survey

want_helping_job.unit: percent wanting a future job mainly focused on helping people or making a positive difference

have_helping_job_among_workers_who_want_.unit: percent of Gen Z adults who want a job mainly focused on helping people and report having one

meaning_job_link.value: Among Gen Zers who find their jobs meaningful, 84% worked in jobs focused on helping people, compared with 44% among those not in helping-focused jobs

mechanism.value: Meaning is not only an attitude toward work; young adults evaluate whether the labor market lets them enact care and contribution through a viable job

observations.method: Harvard Gazette report on a Making Caring Common survey conducted in collaboration with Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation; the public article describes a representative sample of 2,436 people born 1997–2012 but does not reproduce the complete instrument or field dates.
observations.uncertainty: The aspiration and job-alignment measures are self-reported and associational; the public article does not establish whether meaningful work causes wellbeing, retention, productivity or altruistic behavior.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z respondents by age, employment, occupation, financial security, education, gender, race/ethnicity and mental-health status; full subgroup estimates are not supplied in the article.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may find meaning in helping aspects of jobs that are not formally care professions, and job meaning can coexist with dissatisfaction, low pay or a desire to leave.

denominator.unit: Gen Z respondents in the reported survey; public article gives age-specific mental-health shares but not full analytic denominator for every comparison

adult_gen_z_anxiety_depression.unit: percent of Gen Z adults reported as having mild to severe anxiety or depression symptoms in the article's summary

meaning_wellbeing_association.value: Gen Z respondents reporting a recent sense of meaning or purpose were less likely to report anxiety and depression symptoms than those who did not report feeling meaningful or purposeful

care_work_duality.value: Helping work can be emotionally draining while also being experienced as gratifying when people see a positive difference

mechanism.value: Purpose may operate through perceived contribution and social usefulness, but the same care roles can impose emotional and material burdens

observations.method: Published summary of survey associations and interview interpretation; the public article does not provide causal models, clinical diagnostic methods or longitudinal follow-up.
observations.uncertainty: Meaning, purpose, anxiety and depression are self-reported and may be jointly shaped by work, family, finances, health and social support; no causal mental-health effect is established.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z adults in and outside work, including people in caring occupations and people with different financial and social resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: People with better mental health may be more able to perceive meaning, and meaningful work may sometimes increase exposure to emotional strain rather than reduce distress.

observations.period: 2026; meaningful work versus salary and financial security

denominator.unit: Gen Z respondents answering the hypothetical trade-off question; public article does not state its item-specific n

take_double_salary.unit: percent saying they would take a job with double the salary but significantly less meaning and purpose

keep_meaningful_job.unit: percent saying they would keep the meaningful job

depends_on_specifics.unit: percent saying the choice would depend on the specifics

financial_insecurity_effect.unit: percent of adult Gen Z respondents who felt financially insecure saying they would take the higher-paying job, compared with 41% among those living very well

mechanism.value: Purpose competes with material room: financial insecurity makes the salary premium more compelling even when meaningful work is valued

observations.method: Self-reported hypothetical trade-off and financial-security comparison described in the Harvard Gazette article; no realized job-switching or wage behavior is measured.
observations.uncertainty: Hypothetical choices may not predict actual job decisions; financial security is self-assessed and the article does not provide full controls, question order or item-specific sample size.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z adults by perceived financial security, income, debt, care obligations, occupation, education and access to meaningful work.
observations.counterinterpretation: A salary premium may buy autonomy, housing, healthcare or time that creates meaning outside work; choosing higher pay is not evidence that purpose is unimportant.

related_sources.claim: Harvard Gazette summary of the Making Caring Common/Gallup/Walton survey with sample, meaningful-work aspiration, wellbeing association and salary-purpose trade-off findings.
Underlying Making Caring Common report landing page referenced by Harvard Gazette; the record uses the public article's reported measures and limitations.

boundary: This record identifies a meaning-of-work, care-labor, financial-security and wellbeing subtheme. It does not establish causality, clinical mental-health effects, realized job choice, wage or retention effects, comparative generational altruism, employer behavior, care-sector labor supply, or the superiority of meaningful work over nonwork sources of purpose.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Harvard Gazette's official article was reviewed for the August 3, 2026 date, collaboration and representative sample description, 79% aspiration, 56% job alignment, 84%/44% meaningful-job comparison, mental-health association, salary-purpose trade-off and financial-security comparison.
